Subject: Re: Performance SLOs — context window & latency (post-call recap)

Hi Tom / Laura — great conversation today, thanks for the time. Quick post-call recap and proposed next steps so we’re all aligned.

Summary of requirements you called out:
- Primary use case: realtime customer support assistant with retrieval-augmented answers (RAG) for sensitive account data.
- Context window: must support up to ~32k combined tokens (long transcripts + documents).
- Latency targets: p95 for first token <= 400ms; p95 end-to-end for typical responses (<= 512 output tokens) <= 800ms. Streaming UX desired so customers see incremental tokens.
- Throughput & concurrency: expected steady-state ~150 req/s, peak concurrency ~500 sessions.
- Availability & security: dedicated tenancy (Dedicated or Private) and SOC2 evidence requested by procurement.

Key considerations we flagged on the call:
- Large context lengths materially increase memory use and can increase per-request latency due to KV cache and attention compute.
- Streaming helps perceived latency but still needs low first-token time (kernel selection + batching matter).
- Batching improves throughput but increases tail latency; routing policy will matter for p95 SLOs.

Recommended next steps (what we propose):
1) Run a short pilot (2 weeks) on Redwood Dedicated to validate the SLOs at your typical transcript lengths (we’ll instrument p50/p95/p99 and cold/warm scenarios).
2) Engineering scope: we’ll test two approaches — (A) single 32k-capable model instance with prefix caching enabled, and (B) chunked retrieval + summarization pipeline with 8k generation window per request.
3) Deliverables: benchmark report, suggested model/quantization profile, and a runbook for caching/rollout.

I’ve attached the SLO snapshot you gave us earlier and a set of internal 32k benchmarking notes. Vivek (cc’d) added a few engineering notes below.

If that plan looks good I’ll get a statement of work and a HubSpot deal task created. Can we aim to kick off pilot next Tuesday (21 Jul)?

Best,

Hi Tom — quick engineering notes to answer your questions: 

- Warm vs cold: we’ll report both. Typical observed behavior on our 32k-capable variants: cold first-token (after a model spin-up) can be 800–1,200ms; warm first-token (steady worker ready + KV cache hits for prefixes) is frequently 120–350ms depending on batching.

- Throughput impact: going from an 8k to 32k context window increases per-request memory and compute; in our tests that translates into roughly 40–60% lower max throughput on the same GPU class when holding batch size constant. In practical terms, to sustain 150 req/s with p95 targets we expect to need either more GPU shards or smaller per-request generation budgets (e.g., chunk+summarize).

- Streaming and first-token: streaming start time is dominated by the first-token compute path (embedding/encoder warmup + attention kernel selection). At 32k, the attention setup time is higher; achieving ~200ms consistently requires an optimized kernel path (we have a 32k-optimized variant) and keeping batch sizes small for interactive routes.

- Options we recommend for FinCo: 
  1) Dedicated 32k-optimized model instances with prefix caching for repeated transcripts (best UX, higher infra cost).
  2) Retrieval chunking + progressive summarization where we compress the RAG context to an 8k active window (lower infra cost, slightly more complex pipeline).
  3) Hybrid: keep core account history cached as a prefix, chunk longer docs.

We’ll instrument per-route profiling (first token, tokens/sec, GPU utilization) during the pilot so you can validate the economics. Happy to share the SOC2 and data flow diagrams — Marissa, I can attach the standard pack.

—Vivek
Vivek Kulkarni
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
